<reason>Both sides argued at a high level with clean A1/A2 answers to pressure and quotable reframes, but PRO held the motion as written. B's core claim — irreversible, unverifiable ingestion of intimate communications requires prior consent — was never neutralized: A's alternative (risk assessment plus post-hoc deletion/retraining remedies) was credibly dismantled as "a promise made by the taker after the taking," since no one can verify what a model has forgotten. A's best surviving attacks (two-party deadlock, de-identification of free text, provider-exception training like spam filters, grandfathered incumbent corpora) each drew a real answer: anonymization plus orphan-works-style categorical exceptions, "both horns satisfy the rule," platforms with users can ask, and the moat pre-existing the motion. A's sharpest meta-point — that PRO's purpose/beneficiary line smuggles in the balancing the motion forbids — landed but was blunted by B's categorical-exception analogy and the closing that the asymmetry "is the motion." A also incurred two clipped turns, an execution cost. B wins a competitive, well-fought debate.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's Rebuttal 2 (turn 7): answering A's unreachable-parties and spam-scanning pressure with de-identification plus the purpose/beneficiary distinction ("words held to deliver are repurposed to profit"), then sealing it with "consent minus the person" — reframing A's entire alternative regime as paperwork filed by the party with the incentive to take.</best_rebuttal>
